title: Karahan raised Türkiye’s inflation path while describing demand as disinflationary
bank: Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye
summary: Governor Fatih Karahan said the disinflation process had slowed, even though domestic demand was exerting more downward pressure on prices. At the 12 November briefing he put the end-2026 inflation forecast at 29.5%. He also announced higher interim targets for the years from 2027, projecting inflation of 21% at end-2027, 13.5% at end-2028 and 9% at end-2029 before eventual convergence to the 5% medium-term target. The path assumed tight monetary policy and continued coordination with other economic policies. It was a conditional forecast presented by the governor, with no dates specified for subsequent rate decisions (“Medium-term projections”).

The upward revision came largely through supply. Karahan described more expensive energy shipments, longer routes and higher insurance costs. Gas prices had risen more sharply than oil, while disruption, refinery margins and transport costs also affected the import bill. The bank raised its assumptions for oil, import and food prices. It retained the external demand assumptions for both years. Conditions in some trading partners offset part of the weakness in more exposed markets. A persistent shock had also frustrated the improvement in inflation expectations that the bank envisaged earlier. The new forecast incorporated the government’s medium-term framework and announced administered-price adjustments.

The domestic evidence pointed in the other direction. GDP had grown 2.3% year on year in the second quarter, but final domestic demand had slowed substantially. For the third quarter, industrial production weakened while services production increased on data available through August. Card spending had been broadly flat for several quarters. Capacity utilisation was below its historical average and measures of labour underutilisation painted a softer picture than headline unemployment. Most output-gap estimates were negative. Although the bank revised the gap path up slightly, it still expected demand to support disinflation over the forecast horizon (“Economic outlook”).

The distinction matters for reading the next inflation prints. In October annual energy inflation had reached 51.4%, while core indicators continued to ease. From February to October the governor put the increase in energy prices at 43%, compared with 28% for transport services, 17% on the underlying inflation measure and 11% for core goods on an indexed basis. His interpretation was that indirect effects remained relatively contained so far. He warned that persistent energy costs could change firms’ pricing and inflation expectations. Low prior-year monthly readings and volatile vegetable prices could also interrupt the decline in annual headline inflation without establishing a new underlying trend.

The speech documented a substantial change in actual bank funding costs. Resuming weekly repo auctions in August moved overnight money-market rates from 40% to 37%. The October policy cut took the policy rate to 36%. Karahan attributed a cumulative 400 basis point fall in the weighted funding cost to those two developments. Deposit and lending rates had followed to a significant extent, with bank profitability and credit risk affecting pass-through. Short-dated government yields had fallen since the previous report, while longer maturities had edged up. Flexible liquidity provision and bond operations also aimed to manage market stress. The governor treated these measures as compatible with maintaining a tight stance (“Monetary policy”).

The adverse scenario is a series of cost shocks that reshapes expectations despite weak demand. The countervailing risk is that previous tightening and tighter financial conditions slow spending more than the bank expects. Gross reserves had also fallen from USD 210bn on 27 February to USD 161bn on 6 November. Karahan attributed USD 28bn of that USD 49bn decline to the lower gold price, illustrating why the change in the dollar value of gross reserves cannot by itself identify the scale of intervention.

questions.question: What would show that the energy shock has spread into persistent domestic price resets?
questions.detail: The governor documents a larger increase in transport services than in core goods since February, while describing overall pass-through as limited. He does not estimate how persistent the difference will be. That is central to a position sensitive to the next policy decisions. Compare the bank’s monthly underlying indicators and firms’ pricing information with energy-sensitive service prices and successive measures of expectations.

questions.question: How far does the fall in bank funding costs reach actual borrowers?
questions.detail: The speech connects weekly repo funding and the October cut to a 400 basis point decline, but loan growth slowed and retail credit risk was rising. A cheaper funding rate need not lower the marginal borrowing cost equally across products. The governor mentions the report’s box on bank heterogeneity. Its treatment of credit risk, alongside new-loan rates and volumes by borrower, is the next evidence to examine.

questions.question: Which assumption accounts for the largest change in the forecast path?
questions.detail: Oil, broader import costs, food, administered prices and expectations all enter the discussion. The speech gives no additive attribution in percentage points. An investor assessing longer-term inflation compensation would benefit from the full report’s forecast-revision and sensitivity sections, together with the projection vintages available on 12 November. Distinguish changes to assumptions the bank treats as external from changes to its view of domestic slack.

limitation: The source is the governor’s prepared address. The separate slide presentation and subsequent questions from journalists are distinct parts of the briefing.
